
:::callout-tip
##### Key points

- Use SMD (estimated by Hedges' g) or lnRoM for continuous outcomes compared between two groups. Check where every mean, SD, and sample size came from.
- Paired designs need an assumed pre-post correlation to convert the SD of the differences. Change-score estimates (SMCC) are not pooled with independent-group SMDs.
- For before-after-control-impact designs, standardize the difference-in-differences by the pooled pre-test SD (Morris 2008).
- Model estimates can be used when they estimate the target quantity on a compatible scale and come with an SE. Flag them as adjusted.
:::

# The experimental workhorse

These are among the most commonly used effect size types in meta-analyses. These effect sizes compare a continuous response variable between two groups (e.g., control vs. treatment). By continuous, we mean a measurement summarized by its central tendency (mean, median) and dispersion (variance, standard deviation, standard error) across replicates. These replicates are the sample size.

The primary effect sizes that can be calculated with this data are standardized mean difference (SMD) and log-transformed ratio of means (lnRoM). Please see [here](2.1-SMD-assumptions.qmd) for a more thorough description of these effect sizes, their assumptions, and their interpretation. In general, the extraction for these effect sizes is similar. However, as you will see, some data types constrain you to only using SMD because of values ≤ 0 or because of model estimates (t statistics), which only SMD can handle.

:::callout-important

The primary aim of this tutorial is to align extractions with target [estimands](1-effect-size-overview.qmd#sec-estimates-and-estimators) of SMD and lnRoM (see [here](2.1-SMD-assumptions.qmd)).

However, some of the extraction challenges in this page are naturally suited for alternative estimands that account for different study designs. These alternative estimands are not interchangeable with meta-analyses focused on SMD or lnRoM. When these cases show up, we acknowledge the "ideal" estimands but present solutions to allow calculation of SMD and lnRoM target estimands. We also briefly discuss these alternative estimands in the `escalc` [cheatsheet.](6-escalc-cheatsheet.qmd) If your entire meta-analysis consists of these situations, then you may want to use these alternative estimands directly.
:::

# Database design

Download the database template and see the layout advice on [Getting started](3.0-starting-extraction.qmd#database-design).

# Extraction {#sec-extraction}

<!-- ![SMD extraction challenges](figures/flowcharts_diagrams/SMD.jpg){width=60%} -->

## The simple cases {#sec-simple-cases}

We'll start with the simplest figure types, mostly in order to contrast with more complex types. If you're using `metaDigitise()` to extract data [@Pick2018-ia], the function will guide you through calibrating the axes and selecting the top of the error bars and the top of the bars themselves (the mean). If the figure reports standard error ($se$), `metaDigitise()` will convert it automatically to standard deviation ($sd$). Always be aware of what error type the figures (or text) are reporting. `metaDigitise()` converts 95% confidence intervals using $z = 1.96$; for small samples, recompute the SD with the $t$ critical value.

```{r}
#| label: fig-simple-bars
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| out-width: "70%"
#| fig-cap: "Mean and SD of simulated control and treatment groups (n = 50 per group). Error bars show ±1 SD."
#| fig-alt: "Two columns: the treatment column is taller than the control column, and each has a short error bar."

m1 <- rnorm(n = 50, mean = 7, sd = 1.2)
m2 <- rnorm(n = 50, mean = 12, sd = .9)

# Simple:
dt <- data.frame(mean = c(mean(m1), mean(m2)), sd = c(sd(m1), sd(m2)),
                 group = c("Control", "Treatment"))
# dt <-
ggplot(data = dt,
       aes(x = group, y = mean, fill = group))+
  geom_col()+
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean-sd, ymax = mean+sd),
                width = .5)+
  scale_fill_manual(NULL,
                    values = c("Control" = okabe_ito[["control"]],
                               "Treatment" = okabe_ito[["treatment"]]))+
  xlab(NULL)+
  ylab("Outcome")+
  theme_bw()+
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "none")

```

Box plots are also straightforward and involve extracting the minimum, lower quartile, median, upper quartile, and maximum values. `metaDigitise()` will walk you through that extraction and will automatically convert the interquartile range and median to mean±SD using the method of Wan et al. (2014). That method assumes approximately normal data, so check the box for skew before using it. For a median $m$, quartiles $q_1$ and $q_3$, and sample size $n$, the conversion is:

$$\begin{aligned}
&\bar{x} \approx \frac{q_1+m+q_3}{3} \\
&sd \approx \frac{q_3-q_1}{2\Phi^{-1}\left(\frac{0.75n-0.125}{n+0.25}\right)} \\
\end{aligned}$$

where $\Phi^{-1}$ is the inverse of the standard normal distribution function (`qnorm()` in `R`). You don't need to do this by hand, because `metaDigitise()` does it for you. The formula is here so you can see what is being assumed.

```{r}
#| label: fig-boxplots
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| out-width: "70%"
#| fig-cap: "Box plots of the same simulated control (n = 50) and treatment (n = 50) groups. Boxes show the interquartile range, lines show the median, and whiskers extend to 1.5 times the interquartile range."
#| fig-alt: "Two box plots: the treatment box sits higher than the control box, and the two spreads are similar."

dt <- data.frame(group = c(rep("Control", length(m1)),
                           rep("Treatment", length(m2))),
                 Outcome = c(m1, m2))

ggplot(data = dt,
       aes(x = group, y = Outcome, fill = group))+
  geom_boxplot()+
  scale_fill_manual(NULL,
                    values = c("Control" = okabe_ito[["control"]],
                               "Treatment" = okabe_ito[["treatment"]]))+
  xlab(NULL)+
  ylab("Outcome")+
  theme_bw()+
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "none")

```

It's also common to see figures like this with more complex non-independence structures. These can be dealt with by digitizing only the final time point or by controlling for non-independence with random effects (see [here](3.1-universal-challenges.qmd#sec-non-independence) for a brief discussion of these issues).

```{r}
#| label: fig-paired-time-bars
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| out-width: "70%"
#| fig-cap: "Mean and SD (error bars, ±1 SD) of simulated control and treatment groups at three time points. Values are illustrative and no sample sizes are shown."
#| fig-alt: "Grouped columns at three time points; the treatment column is taller than the control column at every time point."

dt <- data.frame(mean = c(10, 12, 12.5,
                          14, 14.5, 16),
                 sd = c(1.5, 1.2, 1.3,
                        2.1, 1.8, 1.9),
                 group = c("Control", "Control", "Control",
                           "Treatment", "Treatment", "Treatment"),
                 Time = c(1, 2, 3,
                          1, 2, 3))
# dt <-
ggplot(data = dt,
       aes(x = Time, y = mean, fill = group))+
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 1))+
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean-sd, ymax = mean+sd),
                position = position_dodge(width = 1),
                width = .5)+
  scale_fill_manual(NULL,
                    values = c("Control" = okabe_ito[["control"]],
                               "Treatment" = okabe_ito[["treatment"]]))+
  xlab("Time point")+
  ylab("Outcome")+
  theme_bw()+
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "none")

```

Let's move on to more complex situations.

:::callout-important

##### 3-dimensional plots

There was a brief unfortunate period in the 1990s when these became popular. 3D plots often depicted multivariate histograms, as well as other data types such as bar charts.

We won't discuss these much here, we just want to acknowledge your pain if you come across one. Hopefully the general plot designs will be similar to those covered in this tutorial. We believe that [WebPlotDigitizer](https://automeris.io/) has options to calibrate 3D plots.
:::

# Raw distributions {#sec-raw-distributions}
## Histograms {#sec-histograms}

It's also common to see the outcome variable of the two groups plotted as separate histograms:

```{r}
#| label: fig-histograms
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| out-width: "70%"
#| fig-cap: "Histograms of the simulated outcome for the control group (left, n = 50) and the treatment group (right, n = 50)."
#| fig-alt: "Two histograms with similar bell-shaped spread; the treatment histogram is centred at a higher value."

hist1 <- ggplot()+
  geom_histogram(aes(x = m1), bins = 20,
                 fill = okabe_ito[["control"]], alpha = .75)+
  ggtitle("Control")+
  theme_bw()+
  xlab("Outcome")+
  ylab("Count")+
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())

hist2 <- ggplot()+
  geom_histogram(aes(x = m2), bins = 20,
                 fill = okabe_ito[["treatment"]], alpha = .75)+
  ggtitle("Treatment")+
  theme_bw()+
  xlab("Outcome")+
  ylab("Count")+
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())

hist1 + hist2

```

`metaDigitise()` luckily has built-in functionality for dealing with histograms. The function will guide you through each step, which requires calibrating the axes and then clicking on the left and right corners of each bar. It'll then convert the extracted distributions into means±sd. This can be time-consuming.

## Violin and density plots {#sec-violin-density-plots}

The beauty of modern plotting techniques has led to a proliferation of new ways to visualize data. Like violin plots.

```{r}
#| label: fig-violin
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| out-width: "70%"
#| fig-cap: "Violin plots of the simulated control (n = 50) and treatment (n = 50) outcomes. The outline is a smoothed density, not the individual observations."
#| fig-alt: "Two violin plots: the treatment violin sits higher than the control violin, and both are roughly symmetric."

violin.dt <- data.table(response = c(m1, m2),
                        type = c(rep("group 1", length(m1)),
                                 rep("group 2", length(m2))))

violin <- ggplot()+
  geom_violin(data = violin.dt,
              aes(x = type, y = response, fill = type))+
  theme_bw()+
  scale_fill_manual(NULL,
                    values = c("group 1" = okabe_ito[["control"]],
                               "group 2" = okabe_ito[["treatment"]]),
                    labels = c("group 1" = "Control",
                               "group 2" = "Treatment"))+
  xlab(NULL)+
  scale_x_discrete(labels = c("group 1" = "Control",
                               "group 2" = "Treatment"))+
  ylab("Outcome")+
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "none")
violin

```

Violin plots are basically a vertical version of a density plot:

```{r}
#| label: fig-density
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| out-width: "70%"
#| fig-cap: "Smoothed density of the simulated control (n = 50) and treatment (n = 50) outcomes. Shading is semi-transparent so that the overlap is visible."
#| fig-alt: "Two overlapping density curves; the treatment curve lies to the right of the control curve."

dens <- ggplot()+
  geom_density(data = violin.dt,
              aes(x = response, fill = type),
              color = "transparent", alpha = 0.5)+
  theme_bw()+
  scale_fill_manual("Group",
                    values = c("group 1" = okabe_ito[["control"]],
                               "group 2" = okabe_ito[["treatment"]]),
                    labels = c("group 1" = "Control",
                               "group 2" = "Treatment"))+
  xlab("Outcome")+
  ylab("Density")+
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())
dens

```

A violin or density plot shows a **smoothed estimate** of the distribution, rather than the original observations. Its shape depends partly on plotting choices, especially how much smoothing was used. This means that the width of a violin cannot be read as a standard deviation, and the bumps should not be treated as individual observations.

The example below draws the same observations three times. Only the smoothing changes. The sample mean and SD are therefore identical in every panel, even though the distributions appear to have different shapes.

```{r}
#| label: fig-smoothing
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| out-width: "85%"
#| fig-cap: "The same observations displayed using three different amounts of smoothing. Changing the plotting settings changes the apparent shape, but it does not change the observations, their mean, or their SD."
#| fig-alt: "Three density panels of the same control observations, drawn with less, default, and more smoothing. The shapes differ across the panels, but the observations are the same."

bandwidth.dt <- rbindlist(list(
  data.table(response = m1, smoothing = "Less smoothing"),
  data.table(response = m1, smoothing = "Default smoothing"),
  data.table(response = m1, smoothing = "More smoothing")
))

bandwidth.dt[, smoothing := factor(
  smoothing,
  levels = c("Less smoothing", "Default smoothing", "More smoothing")
)]

ggplot(bandwidth.dt, aes(x = response, fill = smoothing)) +
  geom_density(
    data = bandwidth.dt[smoothing == "Less smoothing"],
    adjust = 0.4,
    color = "transparent"
  ) +
  geom_density(
    data = bandwidth.dt[smoothing == "Default smoothing"],
    adjust = 1,
    color = "transparent"
  ) +
  geom_density(
    data = bandwidth.dt[smoothing == "More smoothing"],
    adjust = 2,
    color = "transparent"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~smoothing, nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    "Less smoothing" = okabe_ito[["control"]],
    "Default smoothing" = okabe_ito[["control"]],
    "More smoothing" = okabe_ito[["control"]]
  )) +
  labs(x = "Outcome", y = "Density") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(), legend.position = "none")
```

For an SMD or lnRoM, we recommend the following extraction order:

1. **Look elsewhere first.** Check the text, tables, figure caption, supplementary files, and data repository for the mean, SD, and sample size.

2. **If individual observations are visible, digitize those observations.** Calculate the mean and SD from the extracted values. Points may overlap, so use the reported sample size rather than counting the visible points whenever possible.

3. **If the plot contains summary markers, extract only statistics that the caption or legend defines.** A dot could represent either a mean or a median, and bars could represent an SD, interquartile range, or confidence interval. Their meaning should not be guessed from their appearance.

4. **If only the violin or density outline is available, contact the authors.** If the required statistics cannot be obtained, record the outcome as unavailable for calculating an SMD or lnRoM.

::: {.callout-warning}
##### Do not estimate the SD from the width of the violin

The outline is influenced by the smoothing method and bandwidth. Violin plots may also be scaled to have the same area or maximum width even when their sample sizes differ. The width therefore does not provide an SD or, unless the plotting method explicitly says otherwise, a sample size.
:::

It is technically possible to digitize the outline at many outcome values and use its width to reconstruct the **displayed density**. We do not recommend this as a routine extraction method. The variance of the displayed density includes variation introduced by smoothing, so it is not necessarily the variance of the original observations. Recovering the original SD would require details such as the kernel, bandwidth, trimming, and any axis transformation, as well as a separately reported sample size. If such a reconstruction is attempted, label it as an estimated result, validate it against the plotted curve, and test whether excluding it changes the meta-analysis.

# Proportion data {#sec-proportion-data}
## Proportion data (0-1) bounded without error {#sec-proportion-data-no-error}

Sometimes SMD/lnRoM design types will present the total % of a population for a study design that is otherwise indistinguishable from other SMD/lnRoM studies in your dataset.

For an individual binary outcome coded 1 when the event occurs and 0 otherwise, the mean is the event proportion $p$. Its variance and standard deviation are determined by $p$:

$$\begin{aligned}
&m = p \\
&Var = p(1-p) \\
&sd = \sqrt{p(1-p)}. \\
\end{aligned}$$

The expected number of events among $N_{total}$ individuals is $pN_{total}$, but that count is not the mean of the individual 0/1 outcomes. These formulas describe individual binary observations; they do not give the standard deviation among site-level or trial-level proportions.

If you're facing this type of data in your meta-analysis you may want to consider whether SMD/lnRoM are the correct effect sizes for your meta-analysis. This type of data is meant to be analyzed with an [lnOR](2.2-lnOR-assumptions.qmd) type effect size. Alternatively, if these are rare scenarios in your meta-analysis, you may also consider calculating lnOR from these data and converting the lnOR point estimate and sampling variance to SMD. See [here](4-converting-effect-sizes.qmd) for a tutorial on effect size conversions and their assumptions.

Note that these conversions constrain you to using SMD: it is not possible to convert lnOR to lnRoM.

## Mean±sd proportion data (0-1) {#sec-proportion-data-with-error}

Suppose a study measures a proportion for each independent site and then reports the mean and SD across sites. These observations cannot be less than 0 or greater than 1. The boundaries therefore constrain how much the observations can vary, and that constraint depends on the mean.

This mean--variance relationship can make comparisons on the original scale strongly heteroscedastic. To calculate SMD or lnRoM from 0-1 bounded data, you should transform your means and standard deviation to stretch values into an approximation of normality.

The arcsine-square-root transformation does this [@Macartney2022-ik]:

$$
g(x)=\arcsin(\sqrt{x}).
$$

The transformation stretches values near 0 and 1 more than values near 0.5. If the individual proportions are available, transform each observation and then calculate the transformed mean and SD directly. If only the original mean $m$ and SD $sd$ are reported, the delta method provides the following approximation:

$$\begin{aligned}
&m' \approx \arcsin(\sqrt{m})\\
&sd' \approx \frac{sd}{2\sqrt{m(1-m)}}.\\
\end{aligned}$$

The denominator becomes smaller near 0 or 1, so the transformation expands an original-scale SD near a boundary more than an equally sized SD near 0.5. This reduces some of the mechanical dependence between the mean and the available variance.

In `R`:

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true

m = 0.7
sd = 0.1

m_trans <- asin(sqrt(m))
sd_trans <- sd / (2 * sqrt(m * (1 - m)))

c("transformed_mean" = m_trans, "transformed_sd" = sd_trans)
```

This is only a local approximation. In general, transforming a reported mean does not give exactly the same answer as averaging the transformed observations, and the approximated $sd'$ does not necessarily equal their transformed SD. The approximation can be poor when the mean is very close to 0 or 1 or when the observations are widely dispersed. It is undefined when $m$ is exactly 0 or 1.

When the approximation is appropriate, an SMD can be calculated from the transformed means and SDs and interpreted as a standardized contrast on the transformed scale. The sample size remains the number of independent sites, plots, or trials represented by the reported SD.

Do not use the transformed means to calculate an lnRoM and interpret it as a proportional change on the original scale. The arcsine transformation changes the ratio between values. If an lnRoM answers the biological question, calculate it from the original positive means and address its assumptions directly.

Unfold the section below if you want to see a full demonstration of the relationship between means and standard deviation in proportion data:

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

For a proportion $X$ with population mean $\mu$, the population variance cannot exceed:

$$
Var(X) \leq \mu(1-\mu).
$$

The largest possible population SD is therefore $\sqrt{\mu(1-\mu)}$. It is largest when the mean is 0.5 and approaches zero as the mean approaches either boundary. For example, the maximum population SD is `r round(sqrt(0.5 * 0.5), 2)` when the mean is 0.50, but only about `r round(sqrt(0.05 * 0.95), 2)` when the mean is 0.05 or 0.95. A group with a mean near a boundary simply has less room to vary on the original scale.

```{r}
#| label: fig-proportion-bounds
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| out-width: "75%"
#| fig-cap: "The possible population SD of an outcome bounded between 0 and 1 depends on its mean. The blue region contains possible combinations; the dark curve is the maximum SD, not the expected SD."
#| fig-alt: "A shaded region under a dome-shaped curve. The curve rises from zero at a mean of 0, peaks at an SD of 0.5 when the mean is 0.5, and falls back to zero at a mean of 1."

proportion.bound <- data.table(
  mean = seq(0, 1, length.out = 501)
)
proportion.bound[, maximum_sd := sqrt(mean * (1 - mean))]

ggplot(proportion.bound, aes(x = mean)) +
  geom_ribbon(
    aes(ymin = 0, ymax = maximum_sd),
    fill = "dodgerblue2",
    alpha = 0.25
  ) +
  geom_line(aes(y = maximum_sd),
            color = "dodgerblue4", linewidth = 1) +
  annotate(
    "text", x = 0.5, y = 0.46,
    label = "Maximum possible SD",
    color = "dodgerblue4"
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text", x = 0.5, y = 0.18,
    label = "Possible mean-SD combinations",
    color = "grey30"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.25), limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 0.5, 0.1), limits = c(0, 0.52)) +
  labs(x = "Mean proportion", y = "Population SD") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())
```

The curve is an upper boundary, not a formula for estimating a missing SD. Binary observations coded 0 and 1 reach this boundary because their variance is exactly $p(1-p)$. Proportions measured across sites, plots, or trials can have any SD below the boundary. Their actual variation also depends on factors such as the number of individuals contributing to each proportion, differences among sites, and clustering.

::: {.callout-note}
The figure shows the population relationship. A reported sample SD usually uses $n-1$ in its denominator. Its corresponding finite-sample bound is $sd^2 \leq [n/(n-1)]m(1-m)$, so a sample SD can sit slightly above the curve, especially when the number of independent units is small.
:::

:::

::: callout-caution
##### Binary counts and summarized proportions {#sec-callout-reconstructing-binomial}
If a paper reports an exact event count and denominator, such as 17 survivors among 25 animals, those values can be entered directly into an lnOR or lnRR calculation. If the rest of your meta-analysis is of SMD/lnRoM type data, you can convert the calculated lnOR effect size to SMD (but not to lnRoM). See our [converting effect sizes page](4-converting-effect-sizes.qmd).
:::

# Complex experimental designs {#sec-derived-data}
Many studies will present data that has already been partially summarized, such as by taking the difference between paired plots, calculating ratios between means (or paired measurements) or reporting effect sizes themselves. Still other studies may present complex experimental designs, such as before-after-control-impact designs, that require *you* to calculate differences between groups in order to calculate your effect size.

Here we'll go through the most common of these challenges, starting with differences between treatments.

## Differences {#sec-differences}

Some studies used paired designs where, instead of reporting each pair separately, they subtract the paired samples from each other and report mean±error of the **difference**.

```{r}
#| label: fig-paired-differences
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| out-width: "70%"
#| fig-cap: "Boxplot of paired differences (treatment minus control) for 15 simulated pairs. The box shows the interquartile range and the line shows the median."
#| fig-alt: "A single box plot of paired differences, centred above zero."

# Simulate 15 pairs with a pre-post correlation of 0.5
n_pairs <- 15
sd_obs <- 1.2
rho_sim <- 0.5
z1 <- rnorm(n = n_pairs)
z2 <- rnorm(n = n_pairs)
control_pairs <- 7 + sd_obs * z1
treatment_pairs <- 12 + sd_obs * (rho_sim * z1 + sqrt(1 - rho_sim^2) * z2)

diff <- treatment_pairs - control_pairs  # treatment minus control

ggplot()+
  geom_boxplot(aes(y = diff, x = "Difference"),
               fill = "#9BC53D")+
  ylab("Treatment - control")+
  xlab(NULL)+
  theme_bw()+
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(),
        axis.text.x = element_blank())

```

To calculate our target estimand of SMD or lnRoM with this data, we can extract the difference from the boxplot, and convert the medians and interquartile ranges to means±sd (see the box-plot conversion in [the simple cases](#sec-simple-cases)). This dataset would look like this:

| $mean_{difference}$ | $sd_{difference}$ |
|---------------------|-------------------|
| `r mean(diff)`      | `r sd(diff)`      |

To calculate SMD (which is necessary because we are no longer dealing with ratio-scale data and negative values are likely), we have to be creative.

1. Set the mean of the **treatment** group to the mean difference (treatment minus control), and the control group mean to 0.

2. Convert the SD of the differences into an SD for each group (a 'raw-score' SD). To do this you need $\rho$, the correlation between the two measurements in each pair. It is rarely reported, so you'll usually assume a value: $sd_{raw} = sd_{diff}/\sqrt{2(1-\rho)}$. Use $sd_{raw}$ for both groups.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

rho <- 0.5
sd_raw <- sd(diff) / sqrt(2 * (1 - rho))

diff_dt <- data.table(mean_treatment = mean(diff),
                      sd_treatment = sd_raw,
                      mean_control = 0,
                      sd_control = sd_raw)
```

As such your data will look like this:

| $mean_{treatment}$ | $sd_{treatment}$ | $mean_{control}$ | $sd_{control}$ |
|--------------------|------------------|------------------|----------------|
| `r mean(diff)`     | `r sd_raw`       | 0                | `r sd_raw`     |

Since the data is paired, use a paired version of SMD on the raw-score metric. In `metafor::escalc`, this is `measure = "SMCRP"`, with `ri` set to the assumed correlation. The sample size is the number of pairs:

```{r}
escalc(measure = "SMCRP",
       data = diff_dt,
       m1i = mean_treatment,
       m2i = mean_control,
       sd1i = sd_treatment,
       sd2i = sd_control,
       ri = rho,
       ni = n_pairs)
```

Cases like this should be flagged for sensitivity analysis. Change $\rho$ in both places (the SD conversion and `ri`) and check whether the conclusion changes:

```{r}
sensitivity_es <- lapply(c(0.5, 0.8), function(r) {
  sd_r <- sd(diff) / sqrt(2 * (1 - r))
  out <- as.data.frame(escalc(measure = "SMCRP",
                              m1i = mean(diff), m2i = 0,
                              sd1i = sd_r, sd2i = sd_r,
                              ri = r, ni = n_pairs))
  out$rho <- r
  out
})
bind_rows(sensitivity_es)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

##### Alternative estimand: Standardized Mean Change
The example above is ideally suited for a different estimand: standardized mean change. This estimand divides by the SD of the change scores. Unfortunately, it is not comparable to SMD, so do not pool it with independent-group SMDs.

In `metafor::escalc`, this estimand can be calculated with `measure = "SMCC"`, with `sd2i` and `ri` set to 0:

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

escalc(measure = "SMCC",
       m1i = mean(diff), m2i = 0,
       sd1i = sd(diff), sd2i = 0,
       ri = 0,
       ni = n_pairs)
```

:::

## Ratios of control and treatment groups {#sec-ratios}

Some studies report a response ratio directly. Before extracting it, determine how it was calculated. Two similar-looking summaries estimate different quantities.

If the ratio is of two group means:

$$
RoM_{means}=\frac{\bar{x}_{treatment}}{\bar{x}_{control}}.
$$

Its natural logarithm is the usual lnRoM point estimate. To calculate its usual sampling variance, we still need information about the uncertainty of both group means and whether the groups were independent or paired. A single reported ratio without an SE, confidence interval, group SDs, or other usable uncertainty is not usable, unfortunately.

However, a study may instead calculate ratios at the observational-scale between paired measurements:
$$
RoM_i=\frac{x_{treatment,i}}{x_{control,i}}.
$$

The mean of the individual ratios is generally not equal to the ratio of the group means. Likewise, the logarithm of the mean ratio is generally not equal to the mean of the logged ratios. To the best of our knowledge, this data is lost and can't be recovered. Contact the authors or scour their supplement.

If the study reports the mean of the paired **ln ratios** and its SE, use that reported estimate and sampling variance directly when it matches the intended estimand. If it reports an SD across paired ln ratios, the SE is $SD/\sqrt{n}$ and the sampling variance is $SD^2/n$, where $n$ is the number of independent pairs. Do not convert a reported ratio to SMD unless the assumptions and required information for that conversion are satisfied.

## Results reported as an effect size itself {#sec-effect-sizes-directly-reported}

A similar situation is when studies report their results as an effect size itself (e.g., SMD or lnRoM). These could be extracted directly as your effect size *except* that in our experience these studies rarely report a measure of dispersion (sampling variance, or SD or SE which could be converted to variance).

If a measure of error *is* reported then you can use these effect sizes directly or convert them to your target effect size. See [here](4-converting-effect-sizes.qmd) on how to convert between effect size types.

If a measurement of error is provided, then you can extract the data as is, and convert that error to sampling variance. For example, if SMD ± standard error was plotted, the sampling variance is $$vi = SE^2$$.

If a study reports standardized mean differences (e.g., Cohen's d), which is uncorrected estimator of SMD, you can use `escalc` to convert it to `Hedges' g`, the dominant estimator of SMD by specifying Cohen's d as the `di` argument:

```{r}
escalc(measure = "SMD",
       di = 5,
       n1i = 10, n2i = 10)
```

In many other cases, there's nothing you can do but email the authors and hope they still have their raw data.

## Before-after-control-impact designs {#sec-BACI}

Before-after control-impact (BACI) designs are considered gold standard experimental designs. Yet most meta-analyses ignore the before treatment and only extract and analyze the 'after' treatments. Here is a BACI figure, with control and impact (treatment) sites measured before and after a treatment, for example a change in habitat for a plant or animal population:

```{r}
#| label: fig-baci
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| out-width: "70%"
#| fig-cap: "Mean and SD (error bars, ±1 SD) of simulated control and impact (treatment) sites before and after the treatment (n = 50 per group). Striped columns show values after the treatment."
#| fig-alt: "Four columns: control and treatment before the treatment (plain) and after it (striped). The treatment columns rise after the treatment, while the control columns change little."

bc <- rnorm(n = 50, mean = 7, sd = 1.2)
bi <- rnorm(n = 50, mean = 8.2, sd = .9)

ac <- rnorm(n = 50, mean = 7.3, sd = 1)
ai <- rnorm(n = 50, mean = 13.8, sd = .8)

baci <- data.table(m_bc = mean(bc),
                   sd_bc = sd(bc),
                   m_bi = mean(bi),
                   sd_bi = sd(bi),
                   m_ac = mean(ac),
                   sd_ac = sd(ac),
                   m_ai = mean(ai),
                   sd_ai = sd(ai))
baci$id <- "study_1"
baci <- melt(baci,
             id.vars = "id")
baci[, c("type", "trt") := tstrsplit(variable, "_")]
baci <- dcast(baci,
              trt + id ~ type, value.var = "value")
# baci

baci[, before_after := ifelse(grepl("b", trt), "before", "after")]
baci[, control_impact := ifelse(grepl("c", trt), "control", "impact")]
baci$before_after <- factor(baci$before_after, levels = c("before", "after"))
# baci

ggplot()+
  geom_col_pattern(data = baci,
                   aes(x = control_impact, y = m, fill = control_impact,
                       pattern = before_after),
           position = position_dodge(.9))+
  geom_errorbar(data = baci, aes(ymin = m-sd, ymax = m+sd,
                                 x = control_impact,
                                 group = before_after),
                position = position_dodge(.9),
                width = .5)+
  geom_label(data = baci, aes(x = control_impact, y = 4,
                             label = before_after,
                             group = before_after),
             position = position_dodge(.9),
             size = 3)+
  xlab(NULL)+
  ylab("Outcome")+
  ggtitle("Non-problematic BACI")+
  scale_pattern_manual("Before/after treatment", values = c("before" = "none",
                                                             "after" = "stripe"))+
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("control" = okabe_ito[["control"]],
                               "impact" = okabe_ito[["treatment"]]),
                    labels = c("control" = "Control",
                               "impact" = "Treatment"))+
  scale_x_discrete(labels = c("control" = "Control",
                              "impact" = "Treatment"))+
  theme_bw()+
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "none")

```

In this case, only extracting and analyzing the 'after' data isn't a big deal, because the differences in the 'before' groups in the control and treatment are minimal.

However, what about a more problematic result, where there's a big difference in before conditions between the control and treatment?

```{r}
#| label: fig-baci-problematic
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| out-width: "70%"
#| fig-cap: "The same design with a large difference between control and treatment before the treatment. Error bars show ±1 SD (n = 50 per group, simulated). The difference before the treatment persists after it."
#| fig-alt: "Four columns: before the treatment the control column is much lower than the treatment column, and the gap between them persists after the treatment."

baci2 <- copy(baci)
# baci2

baci2[trt == "bc", m := 3]
# baci2[trt == "ac", m := m * 2]
#
ggplot()+
  geom_col_pattern(data = baci2,
                   aes(x = control_impact, y = m, fill = control_impact,
                       pattern = before_after),
                   position = position_dodge())+
  geom_errorbar(data = baci2, aes(ymin = m-sd, ymax = m+sd,
                                 x = control_impact,
                                 group = before_after),
                position = position_dodge(1),
                width = .5)+
  geom_label(data = baci2, aes(x = control_impact, y = 1,
                              label = before_after,
                              group = before_after),
             position = position_dodge(.9),
             size = 3)+
  xlab(NULL)+
  ylab("Outcome")+
  ggtitle("Problematic BACI")+
  scale_pattern_manual("Before/after treatment", values = c("before" = "none",
                                                            "after" = "stripe"))+
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("control" = okabe_ito[["control"]],
                               "impact" = okabe_ito[["treatment"]]),
                    labels = c("control" = "Control",
                               "impact" = "Treatment"))+
  scale_x_discrete(labels = c("control" = "Control",
                              "impact" = "Treatment"))+
  theme_bw()+
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "none")

dt <- baci2[, .(m, sd, before_after, control_impact)]

```

You may also see time series, where the first measurement in the time series is **before** the treatment. This presents similar conundrums. In that case, it may seem like the easiest bet is just to ignore the **before** data but, if there were differences between treatments in the before step, this leads to similar problems.

:::callout-note
There are alternative estimands for this type of study design (Becker 1988; [Morris 2008](https://www.metafor-project.org/doku.php/analyses:morris2008)). If your meta-analysis only includes these study designs, then you should use them. See the `escalc` [cheatsheet](6-escalc-cheatsheet.qmd) for the `measure` options. However, we expect that you are encountering this study design in a meta-analysis otherwise using standard SMD or lnRoM effect sizes.
:::

If you decide to include studies like this, use the pretest-posttest-control estimator of Morris (2008), which builds on Becker (1988). In plain terms: take the change from before to after in the treatment group, subtract the change in the control group (this is the *difference-in-differences*), and divide by the pooled SD from before the treatment. We use the before SD because the treatment can't have affected it yet:

$$\begin{aligned}
&g = c_p\,\frac{(\bar{x}_{post,T}-\bar{x}_{pre,T})-(\bar{x}_{post,C}-\bar{x}_{pre,C})}{SD_{pre,pooled}} \\
&c_p = 1-\frac{3}{4(n_T+n_C-2)-1} \\
&Var(g) \approx 2(1-\rho)\frac{n_T+n_C}{n_T n_C} + \frac{g^2}{2(n_T+n_C)} \\
\end{aligned}$$

Here $\rho$ is the correlation between pre-test and post-test measurements on the same units. Use $\rho = 0.5$ by default and $\rho = 0.8$ as a sensitivity analysis. If the before and after samples are different individuals, use $\rho = 0$.

The extracted dataset would look like this:
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
setnames(dt, "m", "mean")
dt[, trt := paste(before_after, control_impact, sep = "_")]

dt_wide <- dcast(dt,
                 . ~ trt,
                 value.var = c("mean", "sd"))
dt_wide$. <- NULL

knitr::kable(dt_wide[, .(mean_before_control, sd_before_control,
                         mean_after_control, sd_after_control,
                         mean_before_impact, sd_before_impact,
                         mean_after_impact, sd_after_impact)])

```

:::callout-note
BACI designs often lead to negative values from subtracting the *before* treatment from the *after* treatments---which requires you to use SMD instead of lnRoM as your estimand.
:::

The estimator above standardizes by the pre-test SD, which the treatment does not affect, so it does not need the after SD. Run sensitivity analyses that include and exclude this data, and that change $\rho$ (0.5 by default, 0.8 as a sensitivity value).

Compute the Morris (2008) estimate and its variance from the summaries above:

```{r}
n_c <- length(bc)   # control sample size (simulated)
n_t <- length(bi)   # impact (treatment) sample size (simulated)

did_morris <- (dt_wide$mean_after_impact - dt_wide$mean_before_impact) -
  (dt_wide$mean_after_control - dt_wide$mean_before_control)

sd_pre_pooled <- sqrt(((n_t - 1) * dt_wide$sd_before_impact^2 +
                         (n_c - 1) * dt_wide$sd_before_control^2) /
                        (n_t + n_c - 2))

c_p <- 1 - 3 / (4 * (n_t + n_c - 2) - 1)
g_morris <- c_p * did_morris / sd_pre_pooled

vi_morris <- function(g, rho) {
  2 * (1 - rho) * (n_t + n_c) / (n_t * n_c) + g^2 / (2 * (n_t + n_c))
}

morris_results <- rbindlist(lapply(c(0, 0.5, 0.8), function(r) {
  data.table(rho = r,
             g = as.numeric(g_morris),
             vi = as.numeric(vi_morris(g_morris, r)))
}))
morris_results
```

At $\rho = 0.5$ the estimate is `r round(as.numeric(g_morris), 2)` with variance `r round(as.numeric(vi_morris(g_morris, 0.5)), 3)`. Note that you may wish to use a paired estimator for this if the control and impact groups were paired spatially (they cannot be paired temporally).

These 4 group designs may appear in other contexts than pre and post treatment and can be fairly common in ecological field experiments. For example, to understand if reintroduced wild dogs indirectly affect vegetation by reducing dik-dik browsing and abundance, @Ford2015-el placed controls and exclosures in areas with and without wild dogs, predicting that the **difference** between controls and exclosures would be greatest where there are *no* wild dogs. The values below are simulated to show this predicted pattern. They are not data from the study.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ford-design
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| out-width: "70%"
#| fig-cap: "Simulated vegetation response (n = 15 plots per cell; error bars show ±1 SD) in controls and exclosures, with and without wild dogs. The values show the predicted pattern and are not data from Ford et al. (2015)."
#| fig-alt: "Four columns: the exclosure column is much taller than the control column where wild dogs are absent, and only slightly taller where wild dogs are present."

ford_grid <- data.table(wild_dogs = c("Absent", "Absent", "Present", "Present"),
                        exclosure = c("Control", "Exclosure", "Control", "Exclosure"),
                        mu = c(4, 9, 6, 7))
ford_obs <- ford_grid[rep(seq_len(nrow(ford_grid)), each = 15)]
ford_obs[, response := rnorm(n = .N, mean = mu, sd = 1.5)]
ford_sum <- ford_obs[, .(mean = mean(response),
                         sd = sd(response),
                         n = .N),
                     by = .(wild_dogs, exclosure)]

ggplot(ford_sum, aes(x = wild_dogs, y = mean, fill = exclosure, group = exclosure)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.9), width = 0.8) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean - sd, ymax = mean + sd),
                position = position_dodge(width = 0.9), width = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_manual("Plot type",
                    values = c("Control" = okabe_ito[["control"]],
                               "Exclosure" = okabe_ito[["treatment"]])) +
  xlab("Wild dogs")+
  ylab("Vegetation response")+
  theme_bw()+
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())
```

The same difference-in-differences logic above applies to this crossed design. The exclosure effect (exclosure minus control) is calculated within each wild dog level, and the difference between those effects is the interaction:

```{r}
ford_wide <- dcast(ford_sum, wild_dogs ~ exclosure, value.var = "mean")
ford_wide[, exclosure_effect := Exclosure - Control]
ford_did <- ford_wide[wild_dogs == "Absent", exclosure_effect] -
  ford_wide[wild_dogs == "Present", exclosure_effect]
ford_wide
```

The exclosure effect is `r round(ford_wide[wild_dogs == "Absent", exclosure_effect], 2)` where wild dogs are absent and `r round(ford_wide[wild_dogs == "Present", exclosure_effect], 2)` where they are present, so the difference-in-differences is `r round(ford_did, 2)`. A positive value matches the prediction that exclosures matter more without wild dogs.

## % Change {#sec-percent-change}

Sometimes BACI type data is presented directly as percent change, which saves us some of the steps above.

```{r}
#| label: fig-percent-change
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "70%"
#| fig-cap: "Percent change from before to after the treatment for control and treatment groups. Values are illustrative, and error bars show ±5 percentage points."
#| fig-alt: "Two columns: the control column shows a decrease of about 15 percent and the treatment column an increase of about 35 percent, each with a short error bar."

baci.wide <- dcast(baci,
                   control_impact ~ before_after,
                   value.var = c("m", "sd"))
baci.wide[, percent_change := (m_after - m_before) / m_before * 100]

# Customize this:
baci.wide[control_impact == "control", percent_change := -15]
baci.wide[control_impact == "impact", percent_change := 35]
baci.wide[, percent_sd := 5]

ggplot(data = baci.wide, aes(x = control_impact,
                             y = percent_change,
                             fill = control_impact,
                             ymin = percent_change-percent_sd,
                             ymax = percent_change+percent_sd))+
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0)+
  geom_col()+
  geom_errorbar(width = .5)+
  ylab("Percent change from before to after")+
  xlab(NULL)+
  scale_x_discrete(labels = c("control" = "Control",
                              "impact" = "Treatment"))+
  scale_fill_manual("Group", values = c("control" = okabe_ito[["control"]],
                                        "impact" = okabe_ito[["treatment"]]),
                    labels = c("control" = "Control",
                               "impact" = "Treatment"))+
  theme_bw()+
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "right")
```

In this case, use the percent change values directly to calculate SMD. You will not be able to use lnRoM in these cases because of negative values.

The arcsine transformation applies to proportions (0–1), not to percent *change*. Percent change can be negative or greater than 100, so do not apply the arcsine transformation to percent-change data.

# Crossed designs (meta-analysis of interaction) {#sec-cross-design}

## Discrete x discrete crossed design {#sec-crossed-discrete-design}
Sometimes you are interested explicitly in interactions between two treatments. In most studies one of the treatments you are interested in would otherwise be a moderator (e.g., not crossed with the main experimental comparison), however in others you find a fully crossed design.

```{r}
#| label: fig-crossed-design
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| out-width: "70%"
#| fig-cap: "Crossed design: the outcome before and after the treatment (x-axis) for two levels of factor 2 (plain or striped columns). Error bars show ±1 SD; n = 50 per group (simulated)."
#| fig-alt: "Columns for the before and after periods, split by factor 2 (plain or striped). The after-period columns differ from the before-period columns, and the striped columns differ from the plain columns."

# Just use the same data as baci:
baci3 <- copy(baci)
baci3[, control_impact := ifelse(control_impact == "control", "Factor 2\ncontrol", "Factor 2\ntreatment")]

ggplot()+
  geom_col_pattern(data = baci3, aes(x = before_after, y = m,
                                    fill = before_after,
                                    pattern = control_impact,
                                    group = control_impact),
                   position = position_dodge())+
  geom_errorbar(data = baci3, aes(ymin = m-sd, ymax = m+sd,
                                 x = before_after,
                                 group = control_impact),
                position = position_dodge(1),
                width = .5)+
  geom_label(data = baci3, aes(x = before_after, y = 1,
                               label = control_impact,
                               group = control_impact),
             position = position_dodge(.9),
             size = 3)+
  xlab(NULL)+
  ylab("Outcome")+
  ggtitle("Crossed design")+
  scale_pattern_manual(name = "Experimental\ntreatment", values = c("Factor 2\ncontrol" = "none",
                                                                    "Factor 2\ntreatment" = "stripe"))+
  scale_fill_manual("Group", values = c("before" = okabe_ito[["control"]],
                                        "after" = okabe_ito[["treatment"]]),
                    labels = c("before" = "Factor 1 control",
                               "after" = "Factor 1 treatment"))+
  scale_x_discrete(labels = c("before" = "Factor 1 control",
                              "after" = "Factor 1 treatment"))+
  guides(fill = "none", pattern = "none")+
  theme_bw()+
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "right")

```

In these cases, you'll need to record these crossed moderators in separate columns in your dataset. If your meta-analysis is explicitly interested in those moderators, you've scored a major win! If not, then these crossed moderators can be ignored (but should be factored into the non-independence variables in your dataset accordingly).

## Continuous x discrete crossed design {#sec-continuous-x-discrete-crossed-design}

However, sometimes interactions will be between continuous and discrete variables:

```{r}
#| label: fig-continuous-discrete
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| out-width: "70%"
#| fig-cap: "Simulated outcome against a continuous variable for the control group (left) and the treatment group (right). Each point is one observation (10 per group); no error bars are shown."
#| fig-alt: "Two panels: the control points rise with the continuous variable, while the treatment points stay roughly flat at a higher value."

x1 <- seq(1:10)
x2 <- seq(1:10)

y1 <- x1 * 1 + rnorm(n = 10, mean = 0, sd = 1.5)
# plot(x1, y1)

y2 <- 3 * 2 + rnorm(n = 10, mean = 1, sd = .5)
# plot(x1, y2)

dt <- data.table(x1 = x1, x2 = x2, y1 = y1, y2 = y2)

p1 <- ggplot(data = dt, aes(x = x1, y = y1))+
  geom_path(color = okabe_ito[["control"]])+
  geom_point(size = 3, fill = okabe_ito[["control"]], shape = 21)+
  ggtitle("Control group")+
  ylab("Outcome")+
  xlab("Continuous variable of interest")+
  theme_bw()+
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "none")
# p1

p2 <- ggplot(data = dt, aes(x = x2, y = y2))+
  geom_path(color = okabe_ito[["treatment"]])+
  geom_point(size = 3, fill = okabe_ito[["treatment"]], shape = 21)+
  ggtitle("Treatment group")+
  ylab("Outcome")+
  xlab("Continuous variable of interest")+
  theme_bw()+
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "none")
# p2

p1 +
  p2 +
  plot_layout(ncol = 2)

```

In this case, you could extract each point for the control group and the treatment group and calculate mean±SD across the continuous variable. But, if the continuous variable was a key moderator of interest in your analysis, it'd be lost from your meta-analysis.

Alternatively, you could calculate two [Zr](2.3-Zr-assumptions.qmd) effect sizes, one for the 'control group' and one for the 'treatment group'. Group (control or treatment) then becomes a moderator—if this is how the rest of your dataset is designed.

As you can see, there might be no perfect solution. Care and thought are necessary to make this type of data comparable to other effect sizes in your dataset.

# Time series {#sec-observational-data}
## Time series with a binary predictor {#sec-time-series}

Sometimes the data is presented as a time series with a discrete intervention at one point in the time series, such as the introduction or eradication of a species. For example:

```{r}
#| label: fig-time-series
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "70%"
#| fig-cap: "Simulated response over ten years (1995-2004). Blue points are before the intervention (1995-1999) and orange points are after it (2000-2004). The dashed line marks the intervention. No error bars are shown."
#| fig-alt: "A connected series of points from 1995 to 2004, with a dashed intervention line between 1999 and 2000. The color changes at the intervention line."

# length(x1)
x1 <- 1995:2004
status <- c(rep("Present", 5),
            rep("Eradicated", 5))
dt <- data.table(x1, y1, status)
dt$group <- 1

ggplot(data = dt, aes(x = x1, y = y1, fill = status, group = group))+
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1999.5, linetype = "dashed")+
  annotate("text", x = 1999.5, y = max(dt$y1), label = "Intervention", hjust = -0.1)+
  geom_path()+
  geom_point(size = 3, shape = 21)+
  scale_fill_manual("Group of interest",
                    values = c("Present" = okabe_ito[["control"]],
                               "Eradicated"= okabe_ito[["treatment"]]))+
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1995:2004)+
  xlab("Year")+
  ylab("Response of interest")+
  theme_bw()+
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())


```

The measurements before and after the intervention form one interrupted time series. Consecutive years are usually serially correlated, and the five years before the intervention are not naturally paired one-to-one with the five years after it. Treating the points as independent group replicates, or automatically using a paired SMD estimator, would give the wrong sampling structure.

The preferred result to extract is usually an estimated intervention effect from a time-series. If the paper reports only the plotted values, record the time sequence and consider whether a prespecified summary or a time-series analysis is possible. The number of plotted years should not automatically be entered as an independent sample size.

You'll also encounter cases with only a few measurements on one side of the intervention:

```{r}
#| label: fig-time-series-few
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "70%"
#| fig-cap: "Simulated response with eight years before the intervention (1995-2002) and two years after it (2003-2004). The dashed line marks the intervention. No error bars are shown."
#| fig-alt: "A connected series of points over ten years; only two points lie to the right of the dashed intervention line."

# length(x1)
x1 <- 1995:2004
status <- c(rep("Present", 8),
            rep("Eradicated", 2))
dt <- data.table(x1, y1, status)
dt$group <- 1

ggplot(data = dt, aes(x = x1, y = y1, fill = status, group = group))+
  geom_vline(xintercept = 2002.5, linetype = "dashed")+
  annotate("text", x = 2002.5, y = max(dt$y1), label = "Intervention", hjust = -0.1)+
  geom_path()+
  geom_point(size = 3, shape = 21)+
  scale_fill_manual("Group of interest",
                    values = c("Present" = okabe_ito[["control"]],
                               "Eradicated"= okabe_ito[["treatment"]]))+
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1995:2004)+
  xlab("Year")+
  ylab("Response of interest")+
  theme_bw()+
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())


```

In most cases, we expect you'll exclude this data. However, if data is extremely limited you may want to take the mean±sd of the two groups (in this case "Present" and "Eradicated") and calculate SMD or lnRoM. You could also calculate a correlation coefficient (Zr), treating the two groups as $0$ or $1$.

In either case, this requires calculating summary statistics off of non-independent samples. We therefore recommend, if you think this data is essential to include, to conduct sensitivity analyses including and excluding data summarized off of non-independent measurements. See our discussion of replication and non-independence [here](3.1-universal-challenges.qmd#sec-sample-size).

:::callout-important
##### Record the level of every summary {#sec-callout-data-reconstruction}
For every mean and SD you extract, record what it summarizes: measurements across individuals, across space, across time, or a combination. Also record the experimental unit that received the treatment. These fields let you spot mismatched units of replication later and plan your sensitivity analyses. See the callout on [summaries of clustered, non-independent data](3.1-universal-challenges.qmd#sec-callout-internal-non-independence) on page 3.1 for more.
:::

## Time series with error bars {#sec-smd-reconstructing-data}

What do you do if each of these measurements has associated error?

```{r}
#| label: fig-time-series-error-bars
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "70%"
#| fig-cap: "Simulated response with error bars (±SD) over time. Blue points are before the intervention and orange points are after it; the dashed line marks the intervention."
#| fig-alt: "Points with vertical error bars over time; the response generally rises over the years, and a dashed line marks the intervention near 2003."

dt$error <- rnorm(mean = .5, sd = .2, n = nrow(dt))

ggplot(data = dt, aes(x = x1, y = y1, fill = status, group = group))+
  geom_vline(xintercept = 2002.5, linetype = "dashed")+
  annotate("text", x = 2002.5, y = max(dt$y1), label = "Intervention", hjust = -0.1)+
  geom_path()+
  geom_point(size = 3, shape = 21)+
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = y1 - error, ymax = y1 + error))+
  scale_fill_manual("Treatment group",
                    values = c("Present" = okabe_ito[["control"]],
                               "Eradicated"= okabe_ito[["treatment"]]))+
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1995:2004)+
  xlab("Year")+
  ylab("Response of interest (mean±SD)")+
  theme_bw()+
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())


```

In this case, we recommend choosing the time point before and after the intervention and extracting the means and sd for an SMD or lnRoM effect size. This ignores what may seem like an obvious and important pattern from the earlier and later measurements. However, sadly, the observational study design lacks spatial controls, meaning that the pattern is lost to the sea of unusable data. Choose these time points in advance, for example the last year before and the first year after the intervention, rather than the years that show the largest difference.

The example below shows this calculation for the last year before and the first year after the intervention, treating the error bars as SDs. The figure does not show sample sizes, so we use an illustrative $n = 20$ per time point. Replace this with the reported value.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true

n_illustrative <- 20

before_after_pts <- dt[x1 %in% c(2002, 2003)]

es_timepoints <- escalc(measure = "SMD",
                        m1i = before_after_pts$y1[2],
                        sd1i = before_after_pts$error[2],
                        n1i = n_illustrative,
                        m2i = before_after_pts$y1[1],
                        sd2i = before_after_pts$error[1],
                        n2i = n_illustrative)
es_timepoints
```

This gives an SMD of `r round(es_timepoints$yi, 2)` (variance `r round(es_timepoints$vi, 3)`). The two points are measurements on the same units at neighboring years, so they are not independent groups. Treat this as a sensitivity analysis, not as a primary estimate.

# Other reporting formats

## Geometric mean {#sec-geometric-mean}
Some studies report geometric means instead of arithmetic means. If the response is log-normally distributed and the reported dispersion is a **geometric standard deviation**, the geometric mean ($m_{geo}$) and geometric SD ($sd_{geo}$) can be converted to an arithmetic mean ($m_a$) and arithmetic SD ($sd_a$):

$$\begin{aligned}
&Var_{ln} = \ln(sd_{geo})^2 \\
&m_a = m_{geo} * e^{\frac{Var_{ln}}{2}} \\
&sd_a = m_a * \sqrt{e^{Var_{ln}} - 1} \\
\end{aligned}$$

In `R`:

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
sd_g <- 2.5
m_g <- 31

var_ln <- log(sd_g)^2
m_a <- m_g * exp(var_ln/2)
sd_a <- m_a * sqrt(exp(var_ln) - 1)

c("final_mean" = m_a, "final_sd" = sd_a)
```

The arithmetic SD can be much larger than the geometric SD because a geometric SD is a multiplicative factor rather than a dispersion measured in the response's original units.

:::callout-warning
Do not apply this conversion when the reported error is an arithmetic SD, SE, or confidence interval around a geometric mean.
:::

## Means or standard deviations equal to 0
A zero mean and a zero standard deviation create different problems. However this situation is possible with extreme results: every single island with an introduced predator (your predictor) has 0 prey (your response variable). In this case, the mean for the islands with introduced predators would be 0 with a standard deviation of 0.

SMD can include zero or negative **means** as long as at least one group's standard deviation is $>0$. In this case, your data is almost certainly heteroscedastic and you should use the SMDH formulation of SMD (`measure = "SMDH"` in `escalc`). This has to be applied to all the data in your dataset. In ecological meta-analysis, we expect that SMDH is likely the preferred formulation because heteroscedasticity is common (and a subject interesting in its own right, see our discussion of [variability effect sizes](5.1-variability-between-groups.qmd))

:::callout-warning
If both groups have an SD of 0, the usual SMD is undefined because there is no within-group variation with which to standardize the mean difference.
:::

The lnRoM point estimate requires two positive means on a meaningful ratio scale. It is undefined when either mean is 0. Rather than adding the same arbitrary constant, such as 0.01, to every kind of response, you can define the **smallest positive resolution** for each outcome before calculating effect sizes. This is the smallest positive change that the biology, measurement method, and study design could have reported. It might represent one crossing, one animal, one colony, or the detection limit of an assay.

For example, imagine an elevated-plus-maze trial in which open-side crossings are recorded as integer counts for each animal. One crossing is the smallest positive individual value. If a group contains $n$ animals, the smallest positive group mean is:

$$
\delta_{mean}=\frac{1}{n}.
$$

If the reported group mean is 0, it can be replaced with $\delta_{mean}$ for the zero-corrected analysis. More generally, if the smallest positive individual increment is $q$, then:

$\delta_{mean}=q/n$.

A zero SD is an observed statement that every recorded value in that group was identical, so first retain it whenever the chosen estimator permits it. If a positive SD is required to retain an otherwise unusable comparison, treat its replacement as an explicit imputation. For integer counts, the smallest nonzero sample SD occurs when one observation differs from the others by one count:

$$
\delta_{SD}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}},
$$

or $q/\sqrt{n}$ when the smallest positive increment is $q$. This value depends on the measurement resolution and sample size; it is not a universal constant. Because it corresponds to an observable change in that particular outcome, it is more biologically interpretable and less arbitrary than adding the same constant to unrelated outcomes.

:::callout-caution
This is a pragmatic, outcome-resolution-based imputation rather than a recovery of the observed data. Its biological basis makes it less arbitrary than applying one constant to every outcome, but it remains an assumption: a reported zero does not show that the smallest positive event actually occurred. It also changes the reported data and can strongly affect an lnRoM when a mean is 0. Define the rule before examining results. For every corrected value, record the original value, the replacement, the outcome-specific resolution, and the reason for the correction. Always repeat the meta-analysis after excluding all effect sizes that required a minimum-value correction and report whether the conclusion changes.
:::

## Missing error bars {#sec-callout-missing-error-bars}

Many studies report means but do not report error, which can lead to a tragic loss of data.

However, it is possible to use cross-study average coefficient of variation ($CV$) to calculate lnRoM point estimates and sampling variance for studies that did not report error [@Nakagawa2023-tn]. Remember that $CV = sd/m$. Unfortunately, this is far less attractive for SMD, because an imputed SD would change the point estimate itself, not only its weight.

This can potentially retain studies that would otherwise be excluded, provided the means are positive and lnRoM answers the biological question. It does not make the missing SDs known: it replaces them with information estimated across other studies.

Start by checking the article, supplement, repository, and other reported statistics, and contact the authors when practical. Then decide in advance how missing SDs will be handled. @Nakagawa2023-tn describes two average-CV approaches:

- **Missing-cases approach:** use observed study-specific SDs where available and an average CV to estimate sampling variances only for cases with missing SDs.

- **All-cases approach:** use average-CV sampling variances for every effect size, creating a consistent weighting scheme across studies with and without reported SDs.

Neither approach should be selected because it gives a preferred result. Compare them with a complete-case analysis and report the proportion of effects with missing SDs, the CV estimator, and how the conclusion changes.

Since metafor 5.0-1, `escalc()` supports average-CV sampling-variance options for lnRoM through `vtype = "AV"` and `vtype = "AVHO"` (see the [escalc documentation](https://wviechtb.github.io/metafor/reference/escalc.html)). Check the documentation and validate the intended group-specific or homoscedastic-CV formulation before using it.

Let's demonstrate. We'll load a dataset included in `metafor` and set some standard deviations to NA and then use both the **missing-cases** and **all-cases approach**. One catch: the default, bias-corrected lnRoM needs both SDs. So for rows with missing SDs, set `correct = FALSE`. You'll then get a usable point estimate (`yi`) alongside a sampling variance (`vi`) based on the average CV.

```{r}
data(dat.gibson2002)

# First filter out means that are NA
dat.gibson2002 <- dat.gibson2002 %>%
  filter(!is.na(m1i) & !is.na(m2i))

# Set the sd of 2 rows to NA
dat.gibson2002[sample(nrow(dat.gibson2002), 2), ]$sd1i <- NA

# "AV" takes average-CV sampling variances. correct = FALSE is needed because the
# bias-corrected point estimate requires SDs, which are missing for some rows.
res <- escalc(data = dat.gibson2002,
              measure = "ROM",
              vtype = "AV",
              correct = FALSE,
              m1i = m1i, m2i = m2i,
              sd1i = sd1i, sd2i = sd2i,
              n1i = n1i, n2i = n2i)
```

:::callout-note
Note that for sensitivity analyses, you should consider (at least) three analysis sets:

- Using only the studies that reported standard deviation (and using the `yi` and `vi` returned by `escalc`)

- Using the `yi` and `vi` returned by `escalc` alongside the "missing cases" calculations of `yi` and `vi`

- Using the `yi` and `vi` from the "all-cases" method.
:::

:::callout-important
If many of your means are close to zero relative to their SDs (Geary's test, with G' below 3, flags them), you can weight effect sizes by effective sample size, $\tilde n = n_1 n_2/(n_1+n_2)$, instead of by the usual sampling variance. Following @Nakagawa2023-tn, treat $1/\tilde n$ as proportional to the sampling variance, not equal to it, and report this as a sensitivity analysis. See [mean too close to zero on page 2.1](2.1-SMD-assumptions.qmd#sec-overdispersion) for the full discussion. Note that doing so limits you to lnRoM, since SMD requires $sd$ in the point estimator formula and thus requires $sd$ directly.
:::

# Model outputs {#sec-model-estimates}
Many studies report adjusted contrasts from linear models, generalized models, or mixed-effects models instead of raw group means. These estimates are not automatically unusable. An adjusted contrast can be meta-analyzed directly when it estimates the intended quantity on a compatible scale and is accompanied by an SE, confidence interval, or sampling variance.

Do not treat a model-derived SE as though it were the SD of observations within a group. The SE describes uncertainty in the model estimate. When the model contrast itself is the effect of interest, enter the contrast and its sampling variance directly using a generic inverse-variance approach.

| Reported result | Potential route | Information to check |
|-----------------|-----------------|----------------------|
| Independent two-group $t$ test | Convert to SMD | Signed $t$, both group sizes, and test design |
| Paired $t$ test | Convert to a standardized mean change | Signed $t$, number of pairs, and choice of standardizer |
| Adjusted linear or mixed-model contrast | Analyze the contrast directly | Estimate, SE or CI, scale, covariates, and direction |
| Estimated marginal means | Prefer their reported pairwise contrast | Contrast SE or covariance between the two means |
| $F$, $\chi^2$, or unsigned $p$ value | Sometimes recoverable | Degrees of freedom plus effect direction from another source |
| GLM or GLMM coefficient | Possibly usable on its model scale | Link function, coding, adjustment set, estimate, and SE |

The model type alone does not determine usability. The key questions are what was estimated, on which scale, with which adjustments, and whether its uncertainty and direction are available. If those details cannot be recovered, record the result as unavailable rather than forcing it into an SMD.

## From the t statistic {#sec-t-statistic}

Calculating SMD from test statistics depends on whether the data come from a paired design (in which case df = n-1) or an independent two-sample design (df = n_1 + n_2 - 2). This is the formula for calculating SMD from an unpaired, two-sample design t test statistic. It applies to a Student's (pooled-variance) independent two-sample t test. Do not apply it to paired, Welch, or covariate-adjusted t statistics.

$$\begin{aligned}
&d=t*\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}} \\
&J= 1 - \frac{3}{4(n_1 + n_2 - 2) - 1} \\
&g=J*d \\
&Var(g) = \frac{n_1 + n_2}{n_1 n_2} + \frac{g^2}{2(n_1 + n_2)} \\
\end{aligned}$$

In `escalc` you simply specify the t statistic (with `ti`), as well as sample sizes for each group (`n1i`, `n2i`) and use measure "SMD", which will return the unpaired SMD estimate.

```{r}
t = -1.5
n1 = 15
n2 = 15

escalc(measure = "SMD",
       ti = t,
       n1i = n1,
       n2i = n2)

```

For a paired design, the paired $t$ statistic gives you a *standardized mean change*: the mean difference divided by the SD of the differences, $d_z = t/\sqrt{n}$. That isn't on the same scale as an ordinary SMD. To put it on the SMD (raw-score) scale, multiply by $\sqrt{2(1-\rho)}$. This assumes equal pre and post SDs and needs a pre-post correlation $\rho$ (use 0.5, with 0.8 as a sensitivity analysis):

$$\begin{aligned}
&d_z=\frac{t}{\sqrt{n}} \\
&d=d_z\sqrt{2(1-\rho)} \\
\end{aligned}$$

`escalc` applies the small-sample correction and returns the variance for the paired estimate, so you do not need to compute $J$ or $Var(g)$ by hand.

Then hand that $d$ to `escalc` with `measure = "SMCRP"`. The trick is to enter $d$ as the treatment mean, 0 as the control mean, and 1 for both SDs, so the standardized difference `escalc` calculates is just $d$. Supply the assumed correlation and the number of pairs. We show the change-score version, `SMCC`, for comparison:

```{r}

t = -1.5
n_pairs = 15
rho = 0.5

d_z <- t / sqrt(n_pairs)
d_raw <- d_z * sqrt(2 * (1 - rho))

escalc(measure = "SMCRP",
       m1i = d_raw, m2i = 0,
       sd1i = 1, sd2i = 1,
       ri = rho,
       ni = n_pairs)

escalc(measure = "SMCC",
       ti = t,
       ni = n_pairs)

```

**Is this comparable to other SMD values?**

The raw-score version (`SMCRP`) is on the same metric as an independent-groups SMD, so it can be pooled with those SMDs once the assumed correlation is stated. The change-score version (`SMCC`) divides by the SD of the change scores. It estimates a different quantity and should not be pooled with independent-groups SMDs.

## From p values: {#sec-p-values}

When only a two-sided $p$ value from an independent two-group $t$ test is reported, `escalc` uses the unusual convention that the sign attached to the input $p$ value supplies the missing effect direction. Confirm the direction from the reported means, figure, or text before using this route.

```{r}
p = -0.07
n1 = 15
n2 = 15

escalc(measure = "SMD",
       pi = p,
       n1i = n1,
       n2i = n2)
```

## From F statistic {#sec-f-statistic}

For a test with one numerator degree of freedom, $|t|=\sqrt{F}$. The $F$ statistic does not contain the direction of the contrast, so the sign must come from reported means, a coefficient, a figure, or clear text. An omnibus $F$ test with more than two groups or more than one numerator degree of freedom does not identify one two-group SMD by itself.

## Least Square Means (LS Means) or Estimated Marginal Means {#sec-least-square-means}

Estimated marginal means are adjusted model predictions. They are not interchangeable with raw arithmetic means, and their SEs are not within-group SDs.

Prefer a directly reported pairwise contrast between the estimated marginal means together with its SE or confidence interval. That adjusted contrast can be synthesized using its own sampling variance if it matches the intended estimand and its adjustment set is sufficiently comparable with the other included effects.

If only two estimated marginal means and their separate SEs are reported, the SE of their difference also depends on their covariance:

$$
Var(\hat\mu_1-\hat\mu_2)=SE_1^2+SE_2^2-2Cov(\hat\mu_1,\hat\mu_2).
$$

Without that covariance, the uncertainty of the contrast generally cannot be reconstructed exactly. Do not insert the two model SEs into the `sd1i` and `sd2i` arguments of an ordinary SMD calculation.

## PCA scores {#sec-ordination}

Imagine you are conducting a meta-analysis of risk-taking in animals. You are including a variety of behavioral responses: flight initiation distances, vigilance, activity rate, and so on. All of these are considered proxies for risk-taking (and you are of course looking at these both combined and separately because you are a sensitivity-analysis master).

Then you come upon a real stumper of a study. They used a principal components analysis (PCA) to synthesize the exact same variables you are interested in into a single ordination space. The first axis of this ordination space (PC1) has synthesized all the variables you are interested in into a single variable. This might look like this:

```{r}
#| label: fig-pca
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| out-width: "70%"
#| fig-cap: "Simulated PC1 and PC2 scores for five treatment and five control sites (n = 5 per group), with arrows showing the loadings of three behaviors. PC1 is the axis of interest. No error bars are shown."
#| fig-alt: "Scatter of treatment and control points along PC1 and PC2 with three arrows. Treatment points sit at negative PC1 values and control points at positive PC1 values."

dat <- data.table(pc1 = c(rnorm(n = 5, mean = -3, sd = 1), rnorm(n = 5, mean = 2, sd = 1) ),
                  pc2 = c(rnorm(n = 5, mean = 0, sd = 0.5), rnorm(n = 5, mean = 0, sd = 0.5)),
                  group = c(rep("Treatment", 5), rep("Control", 5)))
vec <- data.table(origin_pc1 = 0,
                  origin_pc2 = 0,
                  end_pc1 = c(-2.5, -3, 1.5),
                  end_pc2 = c(.3, -0.1, 0.1),
                  var = c("Vigilance", "Flight initiation distance", "Activity rate"))

ggplot()+
  geom_point(data = dat,
             aes(x = pc1, y = pc2, fill = group),
             shape = 21)+
  geom_segment(data = vec,
             aes(x = origin_pc1, y = origin_pc2,
                 xend = end_pc1, yend = end_pc2))+
  geom_text(data = vec,
            aes(x = end_pc1+0.05, y = end_pc2+0.05,
                label = var))+
  scale_fill_manual("Group of interest",
                    values = c("Treatment" = okabe_ito[["treatment"]],
                               "Control"= okabe_ito[["control"]]))+
  xlab("PC1 (Risk-taking)")+
  ylab("PC2 (Something else, who knows)")+
  theme_bw()+
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())
```

The authors also provide this (though you could extract it from the points in the figure above as well):

```{r}
#| label: fig-pca-pc1
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| out-width: "70%"
#| fig-cap: "Mean PC1 score (error bars show ±1 SD; n = 5 per group) for treatment and control sites, calculated from the simulated scores in the figure above."
#| fig-alt: "Two columns: the treatment column has a negative mean PC1 score and the control column a positive mean, each with an error bar."

ggplot(data = dat[, .(mean = mean(pc1), sd = sd(pc1)),
                  by = .(group)])+
  geom_col(aes(x = group, y = mean, fill = group))+
  geom_errorbar(aes(x = group, ymin = mean-sd, ymax = mean+sd),
                width = 0.3)+
  scale_fill_manual("Group of interest",
                    values = c("Treatment" = okabe_ito[["treatment"]],
                               "Control"= okabe_ito[["control"]]))+
  ylab("Risk-taking (PC1)")+
  theme_bw()+
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())

```

Is this data usable?

Before extracting these means±sd, we recommend looking for raw data or contacting the authors. If these prove to be fruitless, and your dataset is small and hungry, it might be worth using the PC1 scores. However, be certain that the PC axis is synthesizing variables that are otherwise considered legitimate responses in your dataset.

And be careful: you should conduct sensitivity analyses excluding this data to ensure that your results are robust.

**Next:** [Discrete outcomes between two groups: lnOR and lnRR](3.3-lnOR-challenges.qmd)
